catalog_quote: Primary stress is a combination of high pitch, fortis articulation, and length which occurs on each word. One-syllable words exhibit stress. All two-syllable words and the majority of three- and four-syllable words exhibit penultimate stress. When certain morphemes are affixed to words, stress shifts to penultimate or anti-penultimate position: /'piñɛr/ '[a river name]' /'mors/ 'river' /pi'ñɛrəmors/ 'Binyer River' /pičum/ 'far' /-anta/ 'negative' /pi'čumanta/ 'not far' The detailed rules for this shift are yet to be determined. new_statements.quote: Primary stress is a combination of high pitch, fortis articulation, and length which occurs on each word. One-syllable words exhibit stress. All two-syllable words and the majority of three- and four-syllable words exhibit penultimate stress. When certain morphemes are affixed to words, stress shifts to penultimate or anti-penultimate position: /'piɲɛr/ '[a river name]' /'mors/ 'river' /pi'ɲɛrəmors/ 'Binyer River'; /'picum/ 'far' /-anta/ 'negative' /pi'cumanta/ 'not far'. The detailed rules for this shift are yet to be determined. [...] Secondary stress occurs on words of four or more syllables. This secondary stress usually occurs on every second syllable before the primary stress. [note 4, p. 201:] Stress in two syllable words is always word initial.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word carries one primary stress (high pitch, fortis articulation, length). It falls on the penultimate syllable in all disyllables (= word-initial) and in the majority of three- and four-syllable words; some longer words and some affixed/prefixed forms deviate (stress on antepenult or elsewhere), with rules not yet worked out. Secondary stress falls on alternate syllables to the left of the primary in words of four or more syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'Secondary stress occurs on words of four or more syllables. This secondary stress usually occurs on every second syllable before the primary stress' (p. 196), e.g. [ˌari'karikam] '[a type of] fish', [ˌmara'mara'tsona] 'it was yesterday'. Sec. 5.0 (pp. 198-199) adds a phonological clause stress coinciding with the primary stress of one word.
new_statements.exceptions: Only 'the majority' of 3-4-syllable words are penultimate; affixation shifts stress to penult or antepenult (rules undetermined); verb-stem prefixes show no established pattern (/u'rep'okwom/ 'he goes', /'acokwo/ 'he went', /'akwokwo/ 'go!'); sec. 2.2 (p. 193) lists stress contrasts among longer words: /mi'miri/ vs /'mimiri/ (river names), /to'toram/ 'straight' vs /'totonam/ 'dry', /sisi'tona/ 'a sore', /ta'para mont/ 'a scar'. Vowel-cluster nuclei take a single stress on the first vowel (p. 196).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the author defines the word as the minimal lexical unit sayable in isolation, which is 'simultaneously a phonological phrase of one or more stress groups'; when several stress groups occur in one such phrase 'the final one receives heavier stress' (sec. 3.0, p. 194). Data are elicited citation forms and seven short texts from two Air Mati speakers at a 1975 workshop (via Indonesian). Six-week preliminary analysis; author flags it as tentative.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes 'Air Mati' (Airmati), which Glottolog lists as an alternate name of Kwerba nucl1595 (no separate dialect glottocode; the three dialect children are nogu1238 Nogukwabai, sasa1251 Sasawa, seri1256 Serikenam). de Vries & de Vries (1997: 1) treat Airmati-Sarje and Airmati-Sarma as dialects distinct from Kwerba proper (Aurimi village), which is the variety their verb-morphology paper covers. Silzer's data: two Air Mati men (Johannes and Caleb Kwencau) at the 1975 UNCEN-SIL workshop plus one short visit to the villages between the Tor and Apauwar rivers (notes 1-2, p. 201).
